title: A heavy-metal home
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6496, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6496 · constellation Scorpius · about 35000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble shows NGC 6496, a spherical globular cluster about 10.5 billion years old. Its stars are unusual because they hold much higher proportions of metals than stars in similar clusters. In astronomy, metals are all elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.

A handful of these metal-rich stars are variable stars, whose brightness changes over time. NGC 6496 hosts long-period variables, giant pulsating stars that can take a thousand days or more to change in brightness. It also has short-period eclipsing binaries, which dim when a companion star passes in front of them.

Watching how these stars vary can reveal their mass, radius, luminosity, temperature, composition and evolution. Those are measurements that would be hard or even impossible to obtain any other way, so variable stars are valuable tools for astronomers probing a cluster like this.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.81 x 2.66 arcminutes) and distance (35000 light years), the frame spans roughly 29 × 27 light-years. Its light set out about 35,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 through ultraviolet, blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, so part of this picture records light we could never see directly.

explore: Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered NGC 6496 in 1826. It lies in Scorpius, the Scorpion, a southern constellation, about 35,000 light-years from us. The image carries an acknowledgement to Judy Schmidt (Geckzilla).
